## Abstract

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is refractory to most therapies, including immunotherapies, for which reinvigoration of CD8 T cells through immune checkpoint blockade is insufficient to induce long-term durable remissions. Direct KRAS inhibitors (KRASi) have shown clinical promise, although acquired resistance is common. We modeled KRASi response and relapse in mice and demonstrated that, unlike chemotherapy or combinations with checkpoint blockade, an IL-21 cytokine mimic (21h10) induced long-term durable remissions. Its efficacy depends on Th1-polarized CD4 T cells, but not on CD8 T cells or tumor cell expression of MHC class I. Specifically, cDC2-primed CD4 T cells produce IFNγ, which promotes macrophage-mediated phagocytosis of tumor cells. Ex vivo treatment of human PDAC specimens with 21h10 induces IFNγ production by infiltrating T cells. Thus, IL-21-elicited CD4 T cells exert anti-tumor activity in mice and potentially in humans, converting transient responses to KRAS inhibition into durable remissions.

## Introduction

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a devastating disease with a 5-year survival rate of 8% 1. Clinical testing of new therapeutic agents has been complicated by the need for multiagent chemotherapy, usually FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/n(ab)paclitaxel, to slow progression of the disease 2. Evaluation of new agents usually occurs as second-line treatment, where median progression-free survival for second-line chemotherapy is 3 months 3-5. FOLFIRINOX is difficult to combine with other agents due to its high side effect profile, which necessitates frequent use of steroids and G-CSF as supportive care, both of which suppress antitumor immune responses 2,6.

PDAC is refractory to most immunotherapies, including approaches that have produced remarkable results in other cancer types 7-11. The reasons for this are multifactorial, but several long-held assumptions based on mouse models seem not to be barriers in humans. Lack of tumor-specific CD8 T cells due to inadequate neoantigens or too few activated dendritic cells are commonly cited reasons for immunotherapy failure 12-14. However, CD8 T cells are present in human PDAC. CD8 T cells can be abundant and localized to the tumor interior, as shown by immunofluorescence or single-cell transcriptional profiling, although neither density nor localization of T cells is predictive of overall survival 15-17. Second, these intratumoral T cells are specific for tumor antigens, and express similar transcriptional profiles to antigen-specific CD8 T cells in patients with immunotherapy-responsive tumors, such as melanoma 15. Finally, PD-1 blockade induces reactivation of peripheral CD8 T cells, some of which have tumor-relevant TCRs, indicating that T cell priming and reinvigoration with PD-1 blockade occur at rates similar to those seen in PD-1-responsive tumors 18. Although these findings provide hope that immunotherapeutic approaches are possible, determining why human PDAC remains so unresponsive compared to other tumor types has been challenging.

PDAC frequently has KRAS mutations, and direct inhibitors of oncogenic KRAS offer a unique opportunity for treatment. Although these agents are still undergoing clinical testing, early evidence suggests that panRAS and mutation-selective KRAS inhibitors compare favorably to multiagent chemotherapy, potentially replacing first-line chemotherapy in the foreseeable future 19,20. KRAS inhibitors can rapidly debulk tumors, but acquired resistance is common in both mouse models and human clinical trials 21-23. KRAS inhibitors cause massive apoptosis, debulk the tumor, and reduce the immune suppressive pathways driven by mutant KRAS including induction of GM-CSF and myeloid cell-recruiting chemokines 24-26. Immunotherapy has the potential to convert these short-term responses into long-term durable remissions, although which immunotherapy combination will be most effective with KRAS inhibition is unclear 24,27. Combination PD-(L)1 blockade with KRASG12C inhibitors in human clinical trials has been complicated by hepatotoxicity, although this may be a particular feature of the KRASG12C targeted therapies that covalently modify mutant KRAS and can serve as haptens 28. The broader combinability of mutation-selective or pan-(K)RAS inhibitors remains to be determined.

Here we developed a PDAC mouse model of minimal residual disease to rapidly screen known and experimental immunotherapies that could combine with KRAS inhibition and lead to long-term durable remissions. Most agents, including all approved checkpoint blockade immunotherapies, did not extend survival. The singular agent that was able to induce potent long-term remissions was a synthetic mimic of the cytokine IL-21 (21h10) 29. We determined that 21h10 in mice acts independently of CD8 T cells, inducing potent priming and activation of CD4 T cells that produce IFNγ. 21h10 also induces IFNγ from human CD4 T cells, including from PDAC-infiltrating T cells in short-term ex vivo cultures. We therefore propose that induction of effector CD4 T cell responses is a key requirement for converting transient responses to KRAS inhibition into long-term durable remissions.

## Results

### Synthetic mimic of IL-21 outperforms all tested immunotherapy combinations

Direct inhibitors of KRAS, both pan-RAS and mutation selective KRAS inhibitors, can cause profound tumor regressions in mice and in humans with KRAS-mutant lung and pancreatic cancers 19,20. However, these responses are not durable and acquired resistance develops via multiple genetic and non-genetic mechanisms, making combination with other targeted therapies difficult as no single agent encompasses the full spectrum of probable resistance pathways 22. Mutant KRAS is required for cancer cell viability, with potential subsequent effects on the tumor microenvironment occurring secondarily to loss of tumor cells as has been reported using genetic models with inducible extinguishment of KRASG12D expression 30. Here we implanted C57BL/6 mice orthotopically with the poorly immunogenic PDAC cell line 6694c2. This tumor model expresses KRASG12D, has a low frequency of intratumoral T cells, and is refractory to checkpoint blockade immunotherapy 31,32. We treated tumor-bearing mice with the KRASG12D mutation-selective inhibitor MRTX1133 intraperitoneally for 3 days 22,32. At this early time point, tumor regression was already evident, but immune profiling by flow cytometry showed no change in tumor-infiltrating T cells or other immune cells, consistent with a direct effect of the targeted therapy on cancer cells (Supplemental Figure 1). Nevertheless, we hypothesized that immunotherapy could offer an orthogonal approach to clearance of minimal residual disease.

To test this, we established a mouse model to screen potential combination therapies that could convert transient responses to KRAS inhibitors into long-term durable remissions (Figure 1A). C57BL/6 mice were implanted orthotopically with 6694c2 PDAC cells. Once tumors established in the pancreas, mice were treated twice daily with MRTX1133 for 17 days. Tumors regress in this model and are undetectable by ultrasound before the end of MRTX1133 dosing. Nevertheless, residual tumor cells remain viable, given that 100% of mice develop tumor recurrence within two weeks of cessation of therapy. We thus used this model of MRTX1133-induced tumor debulking to screen for potential immunotherapy combinations that, when administered during the 17-day treatment window, could prevent outgrowth of tumors and achieve long-term durable remissions.

Blockade of immune checkpoints PD-1, PD-1/LAG3, and CTLA-4 are clinically approved for use in humans with melanoma and other cancer types, and we tested each of these approved regimens in combination with MRTX1133 (Figure 1B). Although the PD-1/LAG3 combination therapy significantly extended survival in our model, no mice experienced durable remissions. We then screened several investigational immune therapies, including a TLR7 agonist to activate dendritic cells, a cIAP1/2 antagonist LCL-161 that our group had previously reported for its efficacy in pancreatic cancer models 33,34, and cytokine mimics of IL-2/15 (Neo2/15) and IL-21 (21h10) 29,35,36. IL-2 stimulates proliferation of T and NK cells, and IL-21 is a potent mediator of Th1 responses which increases activation of CD8 T cells and NK cells 29,37. Of these, 21h10 was the most effective at inducing durable remissions, with 7 of 9 mice tumor-free at day 90 (Figure 1C). The immune system can control tumors via elimination of all cancer cells or via establishment of long-term equilibrium 38,39. Mice treated with MRTX1133 and 21h10 were fully cleared of their tumors; in a separate cohort of mice with undetectable tumors 100 days after treatment with MRTX1133 and 21h10, we depleted T cells and NK cells, and blocked IFNγ to remove any potential immune control and showed that these mice remained tumor-free up to 250 days (Figure 1D).

21h10 is a de novo designed human- and murine-crossreative cytokine that dimerizes IL21Rα and common gamma chain (γc), which are expressed predominantly by lymphocytes to signal via phosphorylation of STAT3, STAT1, and STAT5 (Supplemental Figure 2A-B) 29,37. Although signaling induced by 21h10 is similar to native IL-21 in vitro, the enhanced stability of 21h10 allows for extended duration of signaling in vivo and makes 21h10 more amenable to protein engineering strategies for targeted delivery 29. Here we confirmed that 21h10 acts via the IL-21 receptor in our mouse model. Il21r−/− mice were fully refractory to 21h10 plus MRTX1133 treatment, consistent with loss of the target receptor for 21h10 (Supplemental Figure 2C). 21h10 outperformed native IL-21, again demonstrating that the enhanced stability of the designed molecule can confer dramatically improved function over the native cytokine (Supplemental Figure 2D).

Pancreatic cancer cells do not express the IL-21 receptor, and 6694c2 cells in vitro were unaffected by treatment with 21h10 (Figure 1E). In vivo, 21h10 had single agent activity against orthotopically implanted 6694c2 tumors, with tumor burden reduced by 50% compared to isotype control-treated animals (Figure 1F). PD-1 blockade had no effect in this model, consistent with the lack of effect of PD-1 blockade in most humans with pancreatic cancer 7. As chemotherapy remains first-line standard of care, we tested whether 21h10 would synergize with any cytotoxic agents, combining 21h10 with gemcitabine/n(ab)paclitaxel or FOLFIRINOX and G-CSF 6,40. Although 21h10 significantly extended survival alone and when combined with multiagent chemotherapy (Figure 1G), none of these regimens led to the durable remissions observed with MRTX1133 combination (Figure 1C-D and 1G).

To extend these findings, we tested 21h10 in additional cancer models. From our previous work on acquired resistance to MRTX1133 in KPC GEMMs 22, we had developed cell lines from a control mouse (KPC3587) or a mouse whose tumor developed resistance to MRTX1133 via amplification of YAP (YAP-amplified). Although we confirmed lack of response to MRTX1133 in vitro and in mice bearing orthotopically implanted YAP-amplified tumors, combination with 21h10 led to 70% durable remissions in these MRTX1133 refractory tumors (Figure 1H and Supplemental Figure 3A-B). Consistent with the well-established role of KRAS in promotion of immunosuppressive cytokines 25,26, both parental and YAP-amplified cells produced GM-CSF and CXCL1, which were abrogated by treatment with MRTX1133 (Figure 1I). These data suggest that inhibition of KRAS, independent of its ability to debulk the tumor, is sufficient to synergize with 21h10. To evaluate the kinetics of tumor regression, we allowed 6694c2 tumors to grow for 15 days and then treated with MRTX1133 or the panRAS(ON) inhibitor RMC-6236 alone or in combination with 21h10 for 17 days. Mice treated with combination therapy experienced deeper and more durable regressions than mice treated with either KRAS inhibitor alone (Figure 1J and Supplemetal Figure 3C). Complete responses were achieved by day 17 in 33% of mice receiving MRTX1133 and 21h10 combination, suggesting that effector T cells contribute to the initial tumor regression beyond KRAS inhibition alone 41. Finally, we tested combination of 21h10 and the KRASG12C inhibitor adagrasib in a mouse model of lung cancer that expresses the KRASG12C mutation (KCP.1) 42. This lung cancer model was minimally responsive to PD-1 blockade and partially responsive to adagrasib, but the combination of 21h10 with adagrasib led to durable remissions in 100% of mice (Figure 1K).

### Single-cell profiling reveals an oligoclonal expansion of IFNγ+ CD4 T cells and a decrease in Tregs

IL-21 enhances the function of activated T cells and NK cells, and it can induce B cells to produce antibodies in germinal centers 37. Our previous studies of 21h10 in mouse models of MC38 colorectal cancer and B16 melanoma showed that B cells were dispensable and 21h10 acted via tumor-specific CD8 T cells 29. To test whether 21h10 potentiated a similar CD8 T cell response in pancreatic cancer, we allowed orthotopically implanted 6694c2 tumors to grow for 14 days, then treated mice for 6 days with MRTX1133, 21h10, or the combination. Tumor-infiltrating immune cells were harvested and evaluated by single-cell transcriptional profiling and TCR clonotype tracking (Figure 2A). Given that the major side effect of systemic 21h10 therapy in mice is pancreatitis 29, we tested whether our previously reported mitigration strategy using TNF blockade could prevent pancreatitis in the context of a tumor growing in the pancreas and whether dampening of inflammation in the pancreas affected anti-tumor efficacy. TNF blockade successfully mitigated pancreatitis in orthotopic tumor-bearing mice concurrently treated with 21h10 and KRAS inhibition, as assessed by histology, serum amylase, and body weight change (Supplemental Figure 4A-C). TNF blockade had no effect on durable remissions acheived by the combination regimen (Supplemental Figure 4D), suggesting that TNF does not play an important role in the anti-tumor response induced by 21h10, consistent with previous studies of TNF induced by other Th1-polarizing cytokines 43. Throughout our single-cell profiling analyses, mice treated with and without TNF blockade appeared indistinguishable (Figure 2 and Supplemental Figure 5-7 29). Global analysis of tumor-infiltrating cells revealed an expected distribution of immune populations, with a predominance of myeloid cells and a relative paucity of T cells in vehicle-treated control tumors (Figure 2B-C and Supplemental Figures 5-6). 21h10 combination with MRTX1133 induced a dramatic expansion of tumor-infiltrating T cells. Subclustering of T and NK cells showed the expanded population was predominantly composed of activated, IFNγ+ CD4 T cells, with a decrease in Tregs (Figure 3D-F and Supplemental Figure 7). Flow cytometry confirmed an increase in activated CD8 and CD4 T cells (Figure 2G-H). Foxp3-GFP reporter mice were inoculated with orthotopic 6694c2 tumors and treatment with 21h10 plus MRTX1133 significantly reduced Foxp3+ Treg frequencies (Figure 2I). Although total macrophages frequencies were unchanged, we observed an increase in phagocytic macrophages, consistent with previous reports of macrophages’ ability to phagocytose tumor cells (Supplemental Figure 5G) 33,44.

TCR clonotype analysis showed that 21h10 plus MRTX1133 induced clonal expansion, predominantly of CD4 T cells with a Th1 phenotype (Figure 3A-C and Supplemental Figure 7). Differential gene expression showed an upregulation of Ifng (Figure 3D-E), and IFNγ and the IFN-response chemokines CXCL9 and CXCL10 could also be observed in serum of mice treated with 21h10 plus MRTX1133 (Figure 3F). Ex vivo stimulation and intracellular cytokine staining of tumor-infiltrating T cells showed increased IFNγ-producing Th1 cells in mice receiving 21h10 alone or in combination with other agents. In contrast, IL-4 and IL-17 production were minimal across all groups. Thus, 21h10 leads to Th1 skewing even in mice where durable tumor control is not achieved. Importantly, CD4 T cells in the spleen were not affected by 21h10, consistent with the lack of systemic T cell activation and relative safety profile of 21h10 (Figure 3G and Supplemental Figure 7C-D). Overall, 21h10 plus MRTX1133 strongly skewed the tumor microenvironment toward a Th1 response.

### CD4 T cells, but neither CD8 T cells nor expression of MHC on tumor cells, are required for efficacy of combination treatment

To determine whether T cells are required for tumor clearance upon treatment with 21h10 and MRTX1133, we inoculated mice with orthotopic tumors as in Figure 1A. During the 17 days of treatment, we also administered depleting antibodies to CD4 and CD8 or isotype controls. Loss of T cells reduced overall survival to that of mice treated with MRTX1133 alone, confirming that T cells are required for durable remissions (Figure 4A). We then tested whether depletion of CD4 versus CD8 T cells affected overall survival. Consistent with CD4 T cells contributing to most of the clonal expansion induced by 21h10 (Figure 3C), loss of CD8 T cells had no effect on overall survival, with 80% of mice achieving durable remissions at day 100 (Figure 4B). Depletion of CD4 T cells, however, led to profound weight loss that required cessation of all therapy after 10 days of treatment (Supplemental Figure 8A-B). Although CD4 depletion cannot distinguish between the roles of effector Th1 cells and Tregs, we hypothesize that acute loss of Tregs exacerbated toxicity. Mice treated with CD4 depleting antibodies had systemic serum induction of cytokines and chemokines indicative of type 2 inflammation (G-CSF, IL-5, CXCL5, CCL12, CCL22 and CCL17), likely as a downstream consequence of the progressively lethal pancreatitis occurring in these mice (Supplemental Figure 8C).

We tried an alternate approach of using mice with genetic loss of dendritic cell subsets. Mice lacking cDC1s and cDC2s were used to determine the antigen-presenting cell responsible for antitumor CD4 T cell priming. Both cDC1 and cDC2 cells were capable of phagocytosing tumor antigen from orthotopically implanted ZsGreen-expressing tumors, as ZsGreen+ dendritic cells of both subtypes could be recovered from the pancreas draining lymph nodes, albeit in small numbers, consistent with previous reports (Figure 4C) 12,45. Batf3−/− mice have impaired development of cross-presenting cDC1 cells, which are required for activation of tumor-specific CD8 T cells (Figure 4D and 46). Consistent with the lack of requirement for CD8 T cells for tumor clearance, combination treatment achieved durable remissions in Batf3−/− mice, similar to the level of wild-type control mice (Figure 4E). Δ1+2+3 mice have impaired development of cDC2 cells, which phagocytose tumor antigens and present them on MHC class II to CD4 T cells (Figure 4D and 45,47). Similar to depletion of CD4 T cells, loss of cDC2 cells increased the severity of toxicity and abrogated response to combination therapy, indicating that these antigen presenting cells are essential for durable remissions (Figure 4E and Supplemental Figure 8D).

T cells recognize tumor cells via presentation of peptide antigens on MHC. To determine whether CD8 or CD4 T cells could induce direct cytotoxicity of tumor cells in vivo, we genetically deleted β2m from 6694c2 tumor cells and tested whether tumors incapable of expressing MHC class I could be controlled by combination therapy. Mice with 6694c2;β2m−/− tumors showed durable remissions with 21h10 combination therapy, confirming that CD8 T cell direct recognition of pancreatic tumor cells is dispensable (Figure 4F). Pancreatic tumor cells do not express MHC class II at baseline, but they can upregulate low levels of MHC class II in response to IFNγ. We genetically deleted Ciita from tumor cells, which abrogates MHC class II expression (Figure 4G). 6694c2;Ciita−/− tumors were controlled by combination therapy equivalently to wild-type tumors, thereby indicating that direct tumor cell recognition by CD4 T cells is also dispensable (Figure 4H).

### IFNγ from CD4 T cells acts on macrophages to induce tumor clearance

Profiling of intratumoral CD4 T cells had shown a striking skew toward IFNγ-expressing Th1 cells. We hypothesized that both Th1 polarization and KRAS inhibition are important for tumor clearance. Tbx21−/− mice have impaired development of Th1 cells and effector CD8 T cells due to loss of the transcription factor T-bet and failed to benefit from combination 21h10 and MRTX1133. Given the lack of requirement for CD8 T cells, these data suggest that Th1 cells are required for tumor clearance (Figure 5A). We hypothesized that IFNγ may be the effector molecule responsible tumor clearance in vivo. Although interferon signaling can induce cytostasis in some types of tumor cells, 6694c2 cells are resistant to IFNγ in vitro (Figure 5B). In vivo, IFNγ is absolutely required for the efficacy of combination therapy, as durable remissions could not be achieved in Ifng−/− mice compared to wild type control mice (Figure 5C). This difference between in vitro and in vivo requirements for IFNγ likely implicates tumor microenvironmental rather than tumor-intrinsic signaling. Flow cytometry of tumor infiltrates from wild type versus Ifngr1−/− mice showed that T cell activation by combination therapy occurred in all mice (Figure 5D and Supplemental Figure 9A), consistent with direct signaling of 21h10 on IL21R+ T cells. However, repolarization of macrophages and other myeloid cells via induction of MHC class II and loss of CD206 failed to occur in the absence of IFNgR1 (Figure 5E-F and Supplemental Figure 9B-D). Macrophages are important downstream effector cells responding to IFNγ. Mice with conditional loss of Ifngr1 on macrophages showed a reduction in the frequency of durable remissions, indicating a partial requirement for IFNγ signaling on macrophages (Figure 5G). One key effect of IFNγ signaling in macrophages is to induce phagocytosis 37. Indeed, we observed increased frequencies of phagocytic macrophages, defined as macrophages that contained lineage-defining markers for non-macrophage cell types 33, in 21h10-treated tumors (Figure 5H and Supplemental Figure 10). To test whether 21h10-activated T cells could directly induce phagocytic macrophages, we used a reductionistic in vitro system whereby bone marrow-derived macrophages were cultured with activated CD4 T cells and fluorescently labeled 6694c2 tumor cells and analyzed by flow cytometry for macrophages that had engulfed the labeled tumor cells. 21h10 increased phagocytosis rates compared to the negative control protein only in conditions where effector T cells were present, suggesting that 21h10 acts on T cells to alter macrophage phenotypic states (Figure 5I-J).

### CD4 T cells from humans with PDAC produce IFNγ in response to 21h10

IL-21 has been reported to increase IFNγ production from healthy human T cells 48. We wondered whether CD4 T cells from human patients with PDAC could directly respond to 21h10. We collected paired peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer prior to starting on multiagent chemotherapy (Supplemental Table 1). CD4 T cells were isolated from peripheral blood of patients prior to treatment and stimulated in vitro with anti-CD3/CD28 in the presence of either 21h10 or the inactive control protein 21AT36 29. IFNγ secretion was increased by 21h10, consistent with a Th1 polarizing effect of this cytokine (Figure 6A). We also performed multiplex cytokine profiling from these same CD4 T cell culture supernatants (Supplemental Figure 12). Consistent with our ELISA results, IFNγ was increased by 21h10. Intriguingly, IL-9 increased upon treatment with 21h10, suggesting that Th9 cells may be induced. More modest changes were observed in GZMB, IL-10, IL-17F, CCL2, CCL4, lymphotoxin, and IL-24. All other cytokines measured showed no significant difference (Supplemental Table 3).

IL-21-based therapies have not yet been trialed in human PDAC. To better appreciate whether human PDAC might respond to 21h10 combination regimens, we analyzed a public database of single-cell transcriptional profiling from 223 aggregated human PDAC samples (Figure 6B) 49. IL21R was robustly expressed by T cells, B cells, and to a lesser extent by myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Figure 6C and Supplemental Figure 12). The common gamma chain (IL2RG) was more ubiquitously expressed (Supplemental Figure 12). To determine whether 21h10 could functionally signal on human PDAC-infiltrating T cells, we developed a short-term culture method in which surgically resected tumors from patients without prior chemotherapy were enzymatically digested and cultured for 24 hours with either 21h10 or the inactive control protein, 21AT36 (Figure 6D and Supplemental Table 3). We successfully recovered viable cells from these cultures from 12 patients and assessed their transcriptional profiles by single-cell RNAseq. 21h10 resulted in increased IFNG from T cells compared to 21AT36 (Figure 6E-F), and calculation of an overall IFNγ response score from all cells showed a significant increase in 21h10 cultures compared to paired 21AT36 cultures (Figure 6G). We performed unbiased differential gene analysis on eight patient samples with high T cell recovery. In addition to IFNG, 21h10 upregulated genes involved in T cell cytotoxicity (GZMB, NKG7, PRF1, GNLY) and T cell activation (LAG3, HAVRC2). Intriguingly, TIGIT and FOXP3 were significantly downregulated, suggesting that Treg loss of functionality may occur in humans as well (Figure 6H-I).

## Discussion

Cytokines can reprogram the immune landscape 37. Of the cytokines that potently support T cell mediated immunity, we found that IL-21 signaling induced tumor clearance in combination with KRAS inhibitors. Although our previous studies of 21h10 in melanoma and immunogenic colorectal cancer models demonstrated a CD8 T cell-mediated mechanism of action 29, neither CD8 T cells nor tumor cell expression of MHC class I were important in pancreatic cancer. In pancreatic cancer, we found that 21h10 induced a clonally expanded CD4 T cell response that was dependent on cDC2 cells and IFNγ and could fully clear minimal residual disease, leading to durable remissions. This CD4 T cell-dependent pathway may be applicable to poorly immunogenic tumors more broadly, and use of 21h10 in other tumors that have been refractory to immune checkpoint blockade is worth investigating.

Acquired resistance to KRAS inhibitors occurs in both mice and humans 50, thereby implying that if a T cell response is generated by KRAS inhibitors alone, it is not sufficient to induce durable immune protection. Nonetheless, direct KRAS inhibitors may combine well with T cell-based approaches. Clinical trials of immunotherapies in the past were designed as either a first-line combination with chemotherapy or as second-line agents where they could be given without concurrent chemotherapy but where the disease burden is high and the expected survival time is low 51. Neither of these types of trials are conducive to anti-tumor immunity, which relies on proliferating T cells and takes time to reduce tumor burden 52. Although T cells can debulk large tumors, they are more effective when combined with agents that cause release of tumor antigens, and in the case of KRAS inhibition, directly relieve tumor cell-induced immune suppression from GM-CSF and neutrophil-recruiting chemokines. The emergence of KRAS-targeted therapies allows the field to revisit many of the immunotherapy efforts that have failed in the past, and revives hope for inducing T cell control of tumors and durable remissions.

Advances in computational protein design and protein engineering have expanded the potential for using cytokines as drugs. Systemically delivered native cytokines have toxicity, and IL-21 is no exception 37,53. The major side effect of 21h10 in mice is pancreatitis, which can be mitigated, without loss of anti-cancer effect, by TNF blockade 29. Another strategy is to design de novo cytokines to include tumor-targeting domains or conditional activation to restrict cytokine activity to the tumor microenvironment and spare healthy tissues 35. These approaches are more straightforward with designed proteins, which are hyper stable and have improved pharmacodynamics compared to their native counterparts 54,55. Fully de novo proteins raise concern for anti-drug antibodies, which can occur for any repetitively dosed biologic, but which may be more frequent against proteins with less homology to their native counterparts. As we previously showed, antibodies generated by 21h10 are non-neutralizing in mice 29. Whether this holds true in humans remains to be seen. One advantage is that only one cycle of 21h10 treatment appears sufficient to induce a robust CD4 T cell response, so a short course of 21h10 treatment during the first cycle of KRAS-targeted therapy may be enough to induce durable remissions in humans. Computational removal of immunogenic epitopes while retaining overall functionality of the cytokine or generation of multiple IL-21 mimics with minimal sequence homology are also feasible with current methodologies 56,57.

CD4 T cells coordinate immune responses and have several potential means of tumor elimination58. Although effector CD4 T cells express perforin and granzyme transcripts, direct cytotoxicity is rare, as is expression of MHC class II on solid tumors. We found no evidence that MHC class I or class II expression was required on tumor cells, thereby circumventing one of the major mechanisms of primary and acquired resistance to immune therapy 59. CD4 T cells, largely through production of IFNγ, can lead to cytokine-induced growth arrest 60. PDAC cells did not show sensitivity to IFNγ in vitro, despite an absolute requirement for IFNγ in vivo. CD4 T cells have been implicated in mediating tumor regression downstream of agonistic anti-CD40 or STING agonists, both of which potently induce IFNγ production 45,61,62. IFNγ has pleiotropic effects on host cells in the tumor microenvironment including activation of CD8 T cells and NK cells 37, although CD8 T cells were not required for the effects of 21h10 in PDAC, making this avenue unlikely to be the major pathway for tumor clearance. Macrophages play a key role in phagocytosis of live tumor cells 33,63, and they are local sources of reactive oxygen species and metabolic competition for tumor cells 64. Therapeutic efforts to target or reprogram macrophages with systemic therapies have largely failed 65. However, local induction of a potent Th1 response can convert intratumoral macrophages to an anti-tumor phenotype while sparing effects on myeloid cells more broadly. Mice with conditional loss of IFNγ signaling in macrophages did not experience as complete a reversal of 21h10 efficacy as was seen in whole body Ifng−/− mice; other cells such as endothelial cells, γδ T cells, or innate lymphoid cells may be contributing to the IFNγ response as well.

IL-21 signaling induced not only an increase in effector Th1 cells, but also a loss of intratumoral Foxp3+ Tregs. Treg depletion may be important in pancreatic cancer, and early trials of Fc-enhanced anti-CTLA-4 or anti-CCR8 antibodies that are purported to deplete intratumoral Tregs have shown promise in mice and in patients with gastrointestinal malignancies 66-68. However, given the overall lack of productive CD8 T cell responses in the majority of patients with MSS-PDAC 9,11,18, it is not clear whether humans have effector cells suppressed by Tregs where loss of this regulatory cell type could lead to therapeutic benefit. T cells in human PDAC may be dysfunctional and may not recognize quality neoantigens 15,18,69,70. Nevertheless, we show that in treatment-naïve PDAC, T cells cultured ex vivo to 21h10 with autologous tumor cells respond with production of IFNγ and activation of CD4 and CD8 T cells, providing hope that 21h10, which is fully cross-reactive with the human IL21R, will effectively activate tumor-infiltrating T cells in human patients.

This study has several limitations. Systemic delivery of 21h10 induces toxicity, which in mice can be mitigated with TNF blockade, but the exact nature of the toxicity profile in humans is unknown. Human clinical trials of IL-21 showed mostly cytopenias and elevations in liver enzymes as the most common adverse events 71. We do not expect systemic dosing of a highly stable cytokine mimic to be safer than the native cytokine in humans, and we are continuing to pursue next-generation engineering strategies aimed at broadening the therapeutic window of 21h10. We were pleased to find that 21h10 could synergize with KRAS inhibition in YAP-amplified tumors, although we acknowledge that acquired resistance to KRAS inhibition via other KRAS mutations or vertical amplification of the RAS pathway 19,22 are unlikely to synergize with 21h10.

The field of cancer immunotherapy has primarily focused on activation of cytotoxic CD8 T cells. We propose that pancreatic cancer in mice and potentially in humans is better controlled by tumor-specific CD4 T cells coordinating innate immune cells. By inducing potent IFNγ+ effector CD4 T cells, IL-21 signaling can potently combine with the debulking effect of KRAS inhibitors to convert transient responses to long-term durable remissions for this devastating disease.

DF/HCC studies #03-189 and #12-013 were approved by the DFCI IRB (IORG #0000035, FWA #00001121) prior to the commencement of study activities. Written informed consent in accordance with federal regulations at 45 CRF 46.117 / 21 CFR 50.27 was obtained from all participants. All animal protocols were approved by the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Committee on Animal Care (protocol #14-019, 14-037) and are in compliance with the NIH/NCI ethical guidelines for tumor-bearing animals. Survival endpoints for tumor studies included palpable tumor measured or estimated to be greater than 1000 mm3, ascites, jaundice, or body condition score less than 2. In all cases where cause of death was unclear, mice were subjected to autopsy to confirm the presence of an end-stage tumor.

#### Mouse strains

C57BL/6 (stock #000664), IFNγ−/− (stock #002287), Batf3 −/− (stock #013755), Δ1+2+3 (stock #037704), Foxp3-GFP (stock #006772); IFNγR1floxed (stock #025394), LysMcre (stock #004781), IL21R−/− (stock #019115), Ifngr1 −/− (stock #003288), Tbx21−/− (stock # 004648) were purchased from Jackson Labs. IFNγR1floxed were crossed to LysMcre to generate IFNγRf/fLysMcre.

#### Cancer cell lines and cell culture

6694c2 β2M−/− and 6694c2 CIITA−/− cells cells were previously published 33,45. Cells used for in vivo experiments were negative for known murine pathogens and were implanted at >95% viability. 3587 was an organoid line derived from KrasLSL-G12D/+; Trp53LSL-R172H/+; p48-Cre (KPC) mouse KPC_3587, a tumor-bearing KPC mouse treated with vehicle to humane endpoint 50. YAP was an organoid line derived from KPC_3323, a mouse treated to resistance with MRTX1133 and was harvested at humane endpoint 50. KPC_3323 had a subclonal amplification of Yap1, which was identified as a genetic driver of resistance by WES and snRNA-seq 50. KCP.1 lung cancer cells were derived from a tumor bearing KRASLSL-G12C/+ mice treated with Ad-Cre virus and were a gift from Kwok Wong (NYU) 42. All cells were cultured at 37oC in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2. 3587 and YAP organoids were cultured as PDO models described by Dilly et al 22. RPMI complete media is generated by supplementing RPMI media (Gibco) with 10% FBS, 2 mmol/L L-glutamine, 1% penicillin/streptomycin, 1% MEM nonessential amino acids, 1 mmol/L sodium pyruvate, and 0.1 mmol/L β-mercaptoethanol.

### Method Details

#### Tumor cell confluency measurements by Celigo

6694c2, KCP.1 or YAP-amplified cells were plated on a 96-well plate (Corning) and treated with 21h10, IFNγ or MRTX1133 at the indicated concentrations. Each concentration had 3 replicates. The confluency was measured using a plate-based imaging cytometer (Celigo) by brightfield. Cell culture supernatants were analyzed by cytokine bead array (EveTechnologies).

#### Western blot analysis for pSTAT signaling downstream of IL-21 or 21h10

CD8 T cells were isolated by magnetic beads and were cultured in RPMI complete for 30 minutes with the indicated concentrations of murine IL-21 (Peprotech) or 21h10. Cells were harvested and lysed in a buffer composed of 50 nM NaCl, 50 nM HEPES, 0.5% NP-40 with protease and phosphatase inhibitors in deionized water. A bicinchoninic acid assay was performed to determine the protein concentration of lysates. Equal amounts of spleen lysates were loaded in 4 to 20% SDS-polyacrylamide gels followed by a transfer to a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane using Bio-Rad Trans-blot Turbo Transfer System. Detection antibodies were incubated in 3% BSA in Tris-buffered saline with Tween 20 (TBS-T) composed of tris buffer, NaCl, and Tween 20. The antibodies used were: Phospho-Stat1 (9167S), Stat1 (11994S), Phospho-Stat3 (9145S), Stat3 (12640S), Phospho-Stat5 (9359S) and Stat5 (94205S). Once images of western blots were obtained, the relative density and size of bands were quantified on ImageJ.

#### Production of 21h10 and negative control protein 21AT36

Designed cytokines were produced as previously described (22). Briefly, 21h10 andor 21AT36 were expressed in Escherichia coli with a polyhistidine-tag on their N-terminus. After expression, Ni-NTA resin with affinity chromatography was used to isolate the polyhistidine tagged proteins of interest. The elution was further purified by size-exclusion chromatography using the Superdex 75 10/300 GL column on AKTA (GE Healthcare). Endotoxin in the samples was removed by washing with 1% CHAP TBS while Ni-NTA affinity chromatography, with removing excess imidazole using dialysis cassettes (Thermo Fischer cat# A52967). The endotoxin in the sample was measured using Endosafe LAL cartridges (Charles River PTS201F) on Charles River NexGen-MCS Endosafe machine.

#### Orthotopic tumors

Orthotopic surgeries were performed as previously described 31. Mice were anesthetized with a ketamine/xylazine cocktail, shaved on the left flank, and the surgical site cleaned with ethanol and betadine. An incision was made in the skin and peritoneum, and the pancreas externalized with forceps. 6694c2, 6694c2 β2M−/−, 6694c2 CIITA−/−, KPC_3587 or YAP cells were resuspended in PBS and mixed 1:1 by volume with matrigel (Corning) for a total of 50,000 cells per 30 μl. The cell suspension was kept on ice and drawn into a chilled insulin syringe. Cells were then injected into the tail of the pancreas, and a bubble was observed. The pancreas was left external to the body cavity for 1 minute with the mice on a warming pad to solidify the matrigel. The pancreas was then reinserted, peritoneum sutured with one stitch of absorbable suture, and the skin stapled with a sterile wound clip. Mice were given analgesia (Meloxicam and ropivacaine) and monitored post-surgery according to protocols approved by the Dana-Farber IACUC. Mice were followed for survival. Survival curves show mice that completed 17 days of treatment and were euthanized for tumor-related end points.

#### Agents used for in vivo dosing

MRTX1133 and Adagrasib (MRTX-849) were provided by Mirati Therapeutics and Bristol Myers Squibb. RMC-6236 was purchased from MedchemExpress (Cat# HY-148439 ). 10% Captisol (Cydex Pharmaceuticals A Ligand Company, RC-0C7-100) in 50 mmol/L QB citrate buffer solution pH 5.0 (Teknova, Q2443) was used to formulate MRTX1133, adagrasib and vehicle. MRTX1133 (30 mg/kg) was administered via intraperitoneal injection, twice per day starting day 4 after tumor inoculation for 17 days unless otherwise specified. The treatments were discontinued before 17 days if the mice body weight reach −18%. Mice that did not complete their treatment course were excluded from the survival analysis. Adagrasib and RMC-6236 (100mg/kg) was administered via oral gavage daily.

Gemcitabine (150mg/kg) was given on days 3, 6 and 9; nab-paclitaxel (50mg/kg) was dosed on days 3 and 9. FOLFIRINOX (5 mg/kg oxaliplatin, 50 mg/kg irinotecan, 75 mg/kg leucovorin, and 15 mg/kg 5-fluorouracil) was dosed on day 3, 6 and 9. G-CSF (filgrastim, 20ug/mouse, i.p.) was dosed daily on day to day 12. Agent Names: Fluorouracil injection (Fresenius Kabi), oxaliplatin injection (Sandoz); leucovorin calcium injection (Fresenius Kabi); irinotecan hydrochloride injection (Hikma); gemcitabine injection (NovaPlus); n(ab)paclitaxel (Abraxane, Celgene). In some experiments, mice received depleting antibodies (150 μg/mouse) via intraperitoneal injection on the day of tumor inoculation and then every 3 days during the 17 days of treatments. Mice were provided with αTNFα[XT3.11] every 3 days starting day 3.

#### Tumor infiltrate analysis for flow cytometry

Tumors were collected and digested as previously described 33. Pancreatic tumors were excised, weighed, minced and incubated in digestion buffer [RPMI (Gibco), 2% FBS, 0.2 mg/mL Collagenase P (Roche), 0.2 mg/mL Dispase (Gibco), and 0.1 mg/mL DNase I (Roche) at 37 °C, followed by consecutive cycles of pipetting, and the supernatant containing freed cells was collected every 10 minutes and quenched at 4 °C in 50 mL conical tubes containing cold FACS buffer (PBS with 2% fetal calf serum and 0.5mM EDTA). Tumors were filtered through a 70-micron cell strainer, washed with PBS, and centrifuged. The resulting cell pellet containing tumor debris and infiltrating immune cells was resuspended in FACS buffer (PBS with 2% fetal calf serum and 0.5mM EDTA) and stained with a master mix of antibodies. Cells were incubated with staining mix for 15 minutes at 4oC, washed once in PBS, and resuspended in 1% formalin prior to analysis on either a spectral flow cytometer (Sony SP6800) or a Fortessa cytofluorimeter (BD). Flow cytometry antibodies used in this study were purchased from Biolegend (αCD45[30-F11], αCD4[RM4-5], αCD8[53-6.7], αNK1.1[PK136], αCD103[2E7], αLy6C[1A8], αI-A/I-E[M5/114.5.2], αF4/80[BM8], αSiglecF[E50-2440], αCD11b[M1170] αCD11c[N418], αGR1[RB6-8C5, αH2-Kb[AF6-88.5], αPD1[EH12.2H7], αLAG-3[C9B7W], αLy6a[E13-161.7])

#### Frequencies of Tregs and phagocytic macrophages

Foxp3-GFP mice (JAX Cat# 006772) were inoculated with orthotopic 6694c2 tumors. Mice received indicated treatments for 6 days. On day 7 post-treatment, mice were treated with Brefeldin A (50 μg/mouse, Sigma Aldrich Cat#B7651) intraperitoneally. 6 hours later, tumors were collected and homogenized into single-cell suspensions (and spleen briefly suspended in ACK lysis buffer) and cell populations were analyzed by flow cytometry. Phagocytic macrophages were identified as CD45+CD11b+CD11c-Foxp3+ cells.

#### Ex vivo stimulation of T cells

6694c2 cells (50,000 per mouse) were inoculated orthotopically into the pancreas of C57BL/6 mice. Mice received no treatment for 14 days, followed by 8 days of treatment with vehicle, MRTX1133 (30 mg/kg, twice daily), 21h10 (15 μg/mouse daily), αTNF (150 μg/mouse every 3 days), or the combination. Tumors and spleens were then harvested and digested to make a single cell suspension. CD90.2+ tumor infiltrates were enriched by magnetic bead isolation (STEMCELL Cat#18951) and ex vivo stimulated PMA ionomycin cocktail (eBioscience Cat# 00-4970-93) in presence of brefedin A (eBioscience Cat# 00-4506-51). Spleen cells were also stimulated. Pooled unstimulated cells were included as negative controls. Percentage of IFNγ+, IL4+, and IL17+ CD4 T cells across different treatment groups were analyzed by flow cytometry.

#### In vitro phagocytosis

Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) were generated from the bone marrow of C57BL/6 mice. Briefly, femurs and tibiae were isolated, and the epiphyses were removed. Bone marrow cells were flushed out using a 27G needle (BD, Cat# 305109) and sterile PBS. The collected cells were passed through a 70 μm cell strainer, centrifuged at 300 × g for 5 min, and resuspended in RPMI complete supplemented with mouse macrophage colony-stimulating factor (20 ng/mL mM-CSF) (PeproTech, Cat# 305-02). Cells were plated on 150 × 15 mm petri dishes at a concentration of 0.5 million cells per ml and incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2. The medium was refreshed every other day, and fully differentiated macrophages were used for experiments on Day 6 and resended in 24 well plates at 50,000 cells per well.

CD4 T cells were obtained from spleen and inguinal lymph nodes and mechanically homogenized through 40-μm filters. CD8 T cells were isolated via magnetic bead enrichment with an EasySep Mouse CD4+ T cell isolation kit (STEMCELL Technologies, catalog no. 19825). CD4 T cells were cultured at 1 million per ml in a 12-well plate coated with PBS or 1ug/ml antiCD3 in RPMI complete media composed of RPMI 1640 media (Life Technologies, 11875119) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 1 mM sodium pyruvate (Gibco, catalog no. 11360070), 2 mM GlutaMAX (Gibco, catalog no.35050061), 0.1 mM nonessential amino acids (Gibco, catalog no. 11140050), penicillin/streptomycin (100 U/ml; Gibco, catalog no. 15140122), and 0.11 M β-mercaptoethanol (Sigma-Aldrich, M3148), along with 100 U/ml IL2 and 1nM 21H10 or 21AT36. Fresh medium with 100 U/ml IL2 and 1nM 21H10 or 21AT36 are provided every other day until day 6.

6694C2 tumor cells are stained with CTV (Fisher Scientific, Cat# C34557) and 50,000 CTV-stained tumor cells are seeded on top of 50,000 macrophages along with 2 fold diluted T cell supernatant and 50,000 T cells in various conditions and cultured for 20 hrs. All the cells are harvested and stained with anti-CD11b antibody (M1/70). Percetage of phagocytic macrophages are analyzed by flow cytometry.

#### Single-cell RNA-sequencing preparation

Mice bearing orthotopically implanted 6694c2 tumors were sacrificed at 21 days post-tumor inoculation. Tumors were collected from mice and digested as described above. The single cell suspension containing tumor debris and infiltrating immune cells was resuspended in FACS buffer (PBS with 2% fetal calf serum and 0.5 mM EDTA) and incubated with CD45 Stemcell Easysep beads (Stemcell Cat# 18945). Following the manufacturer’s protocol, magnetically enriched CD45+ populations were collected and counted with a hemocytometer. For each tumor from a treatment group, a different TotalSeqC hashing antibody (mouse Hashtags 1-5, Biolegend) was incubated with 2 μL Ab/million cells in PBS (with 2% FBS) for 20 minutes at 4°C. Following three washes with 0.05% ultrapure BSA (Invitrogen Cat# AM2618) in PBS, cells were counted again and resuspended at 1,000 cells/μL. Approximately 4,000 cells/tumor were pooled across each treatment group (five hashtags/treatment group) and loaded onto a 10X Chromium Controller with a Single Cell K Chip (PN-2000182) using the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 5' GEM Kit v2 reagents and beads (PN-1000244 and PN-1000264).

Human PDAC tumor sections and biopsy bites were collected from treatment-naïve patients with PDAC under protocol #03-189 (see Supplemental Table 2). Upon receiving fresh tumor, tissues were immediately collected into DMEM media on ice then minced into 1-2 mm3 cubes before putting into freezing media (10% DMSO; 40% RPMI; 50% FBS) and frozen. Frozen and thawed tissue was then manually dissociated with a sterile razor and transferred to pre-warmed 37°C digestion enzyme mix in RPMI (Miltenyi tumor dissociation kit, cat. 130-095-929). In a 37°C water bath, tissue digestion was agitated every 2 minutes, and pipetted up and down every 10 minutes for a total of 30 minutes. Digested tissue was filtered through a 70μM strainer, washed with RPMI containing 10% FBS, and the single-cell suspension was collected and processed for ex-vivo culture. Equal amount of cells from the same patient were treated with 21H10 or 21AT36 in RPMI complete media for 24 hours, with or without 10 U/mL IL-2 as indicated. Then samples were incubated with TotalSeqC hashing antibody (Biolengend) with 2 μL Ab/million cells in PBS (with 2% FBS) for 20 minutes at 4°C. Following three washes with 0.05% ultrapure BSA (Invitrogen Cat# AM2618) in PBS, cells were counted again, resuspended at 1,000 cells/μL and loaded onto a 10X Chromium Controller with a Single Cell K Chip using the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 5' GEM Kit v2 reagents and beads.

Library preparation was performed with the Library Construction Kit (PN-1000190) to generate gene expression libraries and 5’ Feature Barcode kit (PN-1000256) was used to generate hashtag libraries. Samples were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 instrument with 2x150bp sequencing (Azenta Life Sciences).

#### Single-cell RNA-sequencing pre-processing

The 10x Cellranger pipeline (v7.0.0) was used to align reads to the hg38 Homo sapiens genome or mm10 Mus musculus genome (from 10x Genomics). The GRCh38 Human V(D)J Reference (v7.1.0) and GRCm38 Human V(D)J Reference (v7.0.0) was downloaded from 10x Genomics and used with Cellranger ‘multi’ to profile the TCR repertoire of samples. The count matrices were imported for downstream analysis into R using the Seurat (v4.3.0) package. The DropletUtils (v1.18.1) package was used to exclude empty droplets54 from the count matrices with an FDR <0.01 and genes expressed in fewer than 3 cells were excluded. Hashtag reads were used to demultiplex samples with the Seurat ‘HTODemux’ function, using a kmeans function with “nstarts = 30” and a 99% positive quantile threshold. Only cells classified as a “singlet” but not as a “doublet” or “negative” by hashtag demultiplexing were kept for downstream analysis. Following hash demultiplexing, cells expressing fewer than 500 transcripts and 200 total genes were removed, as were cells with mitochondrial gene expression percentages greater than 2 MADs above the median (med+2MAD). Three samples with med+2MAD > 20% had their cutoff set to 10%. Data from each sample was log-normalized, and 2000 variable features from each sample were identified.

#### Single-cell RNA-sequencing clustering

Each filtered, demultiplexed sample was log normalized, and 2,000 variable features were identified and used to find 3,000 integration features to combine samples to minimize batch effects. The newly integrated dataset was scaled, and a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed, from which the top 25 PCs were used for uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) generation. From the 25 PCs, a shared nearest neighbor (SNN) graph was constructed (k = 20 neighbors), and clusters were classified by the Louvain algorithm. The ‘FindAllMarkers’ function was used to find the top cluster-defining genes, and these gene lists were used to assign cell types. Human PDAC atlas from Loveless et al. (EGAS00001002543, GSE154778, GSE155698, GSE156405, GSE158356, GSE194247, GSE202051, GSE205013, GSE211644, GSE229413, phs001840.v1.p1, and PRJCA001063, available at https://zenodo.org/records/14199536) was analyzed in the same way.

#### Differential gene expression analysis

Across each T cell and macrophage sub-cluster, we performed a pseudo-bulk method of differential gene expression analysis for both mouse and human samples 72,73. Each mouse within a treatment group was treated as a replicate, and count matrices were summed across genes for each sub-cluster per mouse. Using the DESeq2 (v1.38.3) package 74 and pseudo-bulk gene expression values, differentially expressed genes were identified across treatment groups and sub-clusters. Similarly, we performed a pseudo-bulk method of differential gene expression analysis for n=8 patients that have over 100 T cell, comparing the 21h10 treated samples to 21AT36 samples. Raw UMI counts from all T cells within each patient-treatment sample were aggregated to generate one pseudobulk count profile per biological sample (16 pseudobulk samples total). Differential expression between 21H10 and 21AT36 treatment was performed using DESeq2 with a paired design (~ patient + treatment), treating patients as the biological replicates. For IFNγ signature analysis, expression of genes from the Hallmark IFNγ response gene set (MSigDB v2023.2) was extracted from the seurat object. Gene expression was Z-score normalized across all cells, and IFNγ signature score was calculated by summing scaled expression values per cell.

#### Human PDAC peripheral blood samples and ex vivo cultures

Whole blood was collected from treatment-naïve patients with PDAC under protocol #03-189 (see Table 2). Whole blood was processed within 24 hours of collection. From the fresh whole blood, 200 μl were used for flow cytometry staining. The remaining blood was used for PBMC isolation by gradient centrifugation using Ficoll-paque™plus (Cytiva). Cells were frozen in 90% FBS (Gibco)/ 10% DMSO (Dimethyl sulfoxide) (Sigma-Aldrich) at a maximum concentration of 5x106cells/mL and stored in liquid nitrogen. Frozen PBMCs were thawed in a warm bath and then placed in 10 mL of a solution of RPMIc with DNase I (Sigma Aldrich). PBMCs were washed once in RPMI complete. CD4T cells were isolated from 5 million of PBMCs collected from treatment-naïve patients with PDAC by EasySep (StemCell #17952) and plated on a 96-well plate (Corning). Equal numbers of cells from the same patient were treated with aCD3/CD28 along with 10 nM of 21h10 or 21AT36 in RPMI complete media for 2 days. Cell supernatants were collected after 2 days and human IFNγ level was quantified using BioLegend’s enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) MAX Deluxe set (#430104). The supernatants were analyzed by cytokine bead array (EveTechnologies).

#### Quantification and Statistical Analysis

Statistical details of experiments can be found in each of the figure legends which include the statistical tests used and exact value of n representing biological replicates. The center is always shown as the mean, with individual data points indicated in the figure art for groups with n<10 biological replicates. Error bars represent SEM. Confidence intervals are not shown.

Pairwise, group comparisons and correlations were performed using Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test and non-parametric one-way ANOVA test. Data were not assumed to have a normal distribution. Survival analyses were performed using a Log rank Mantel-Cox test. GraphPad PRISM software was used for statistical analysis.
